newsitem.title: GERMANY: German SPD's Schroeder calls for delay of EMU.
newsitem.headline: German SPD's Schroeder calls for delay of EMU.

text.p: The planned launch of Europe's single currency in 1999 should be delayed as Germany will not qualify in time without creative accounting, a leading member of Germany's Social Democrat (SPD) opposition party said in newspaper interviews published on Monday.

Gerhard Schroeder, premier of the state of Lower Saxony and tipped as contender for the chancellorship in the 1998 general election, told the Financial Times he did not believe a delay would be damaging to Europe in the long run.
"The integration process is so far advanced that I don't believe it would come to a halt if we said: 'We won't make it in 1999, we will delay it.'"
Schroeder was also quoted as saying that while the Maastricht Treaty and the idea behind it were in order, the real problem was that it had to be implemented in such a tight timescale.
The need to maintain strict adherence to the convergence criteria forced Germany to "give up all means of intervention" that could reduce German unemployment, now at a post-war record.

Schroeder frequently warns of the risks entailed in launching the single currency, or euro, and in December faced a storm of criticism from government politicians after he declared the currency was bound to be weaker than the mark.
In a separate newspaper interview published on Monday, Schroeder said that Maastricht had not strictly set January 1, 1999 as the launch date for the euro.

"Strictly speaking the partners have not even committed themselves because the euro will only be introduced if nothing has been decided by the end of the year. So we still have possibilities to intervene," Schroeder told the Frankfurter Neue Presse.

A steady rise in unemployment this year has raised doubts that Germany will be able to meet the key budget criterion under which states must keep their deficit below three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) to qualify for the euro.

Schroeder said that while experts at commercial banks were warning against a launch in 1999, their superiors on the management boards were "throwing caution to the wind - because of political correctness and because of the investments they have made."

He noted that the presidents of the savings bank association and co-operative banking association, Horst Koehler and Wolfgang Grueger respectively, had their ears close to the "Mittelstand", the medium-sized business sector, and to the needs of savers and had said a delay would be tolerable.
Schroeder also said that public debate about the euro was underdeveloped in Germany compared with the more vigorous discussion in Britain, France and Italy.
Separately, Schroeder did not rule out the possibility of a "grand coalition" between the SPD and the ruling Christian Democrats (CDU) to overcome Germany's problems.

"Put it this way. One and a half years before a general election, there is not much point speculating about a grand coalition. But one should not be worried about it. The SPD must be prepared to treat it as a political option," he told the Financial Times.
